summary: Microsoft completed its $69bn (£56bn) acquisition of Activision Blizzard, and the article explains what it means for gamers. Call of Duty can't be an Xbox-exclusive before 2038 because Ubisoft holds 15-year cloud gaming rights, a condition imposed by UK regulators. Activision titles are expected on Game Pass from next year, and Microsoft gains from in-game purchases even on PlayStation. Fan reactions are mixed, and the deal puts more UK studios under Microsoft's control.
one_line: Microsoft closed its $69bn Activision Blizzard purchase; Call of Duty stays on PlayStation for now, Game Pass additions are expected, and fans are divided.
key_facts: Microsoft paid $69bn (£56bn) to complete its deal for Activision Blizzard.
Call of Duty is one of the biggest-selling video game franchises of all time, behind only Mario, Tetris and Pokemon.
It will be 2038 before Call of Duty could possibly become an Xbox exclusive.

Ubisoft signed a deal giving it cloud gaming rights for every Activision Blizzard game, past and future, for 15 years; Microsoft agreed to this to get past UK regulators worried about cloud industry dominance.
Activision Blizzard said in a post on X that it expects to start adding its titles to Game Pass next year, so the new Call of Duty may be playable on Xbox from day one.
Starfield, from Microsoft-owned Bethesda, launched in September 2023 exclusively on PC and Xbox and was playable on Game Pass from day one.
According to Statista, Activision Blizzard made $5.89bn in 2022 from microtransactions, downloadable content and royalties, versus $1.6bn from selling games.
Sony takes around a 30% cut of in-game purchases, so Call of Duty purchases on PlayStation will now fund a rival.
Some fans have started petitions asking Microsoft to keep the games on all consoles in perpetuity, recalling when Crash Bandicoot and Spyro the Dragon were PlayStation exclusives.
Activision Blizzard has studios in London, Guildford and Warrington, and owns King, maker of Candy Crush Saga, based in Stockholm and London.
Ukie says 89% of total investment in the UK games industry between January 2017 and June 2022 came from non-UK companies.
Microsoft bought Rare for $375m in 2002 and Mojang, maker of Minecraft, for $2.5bn in 2014.
Microsoft now owns more than 20 gaming studios; newly acquired franchises include Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, World of Warcraft, Diablo, Overwatch and Candy Crush Saga.
